nodes.question: How many bird species are hosted by the Cakalburnu Lagoon?
nodes.answer: The Cakalburnu Lagoon hosts 121 bird species.
nodes.paragraph: In 2019, the amount of green space per person in Izmir city is 8.6 m2 (Ersoy-Tonyalo lu & Nurlu, 2023). The Cakalburnu Lagoon has experienced a 5.6% loss in Water Air Soil Pollut (2025) 236:208 208 Vol. : (123456789) land use area over a 22-year period between 1996 and 2018 (Kara, 2019). Cakalburnu Lagoon is the most important element of the wetland and hosts 121 bird species (Kaya, 2017). Lagoon systems, in addition to being natural bio- logical resources, serve as natural laboratories for scientific research and play a significant role in the preservation and sustainability of biodiversity in sensitive and fragile ecosystems (Yucel-Gier et al., 2018). The quantity and quality of water in a lagoon are influenced by factors such as evaporation within the lagoon, precipitation, groundwater inflow, sur - face runoff, and the exchange of seawater (Somay, 2016; Somay-Altas, 2021). The Cakalburnu Lagoon is an irreplaceable coastal urban wetland located to the south of Izmir Bay, encompasses an area of approximately 64 hectares and exhibits a shallow depth ranging from 0.5 to 1 m. A reforestation pro- ject in the northern part of the Cakalburnu Lagoon, situated within the study area, has led to the establish- ment of the Izmir-Inciralt Recreation Area cover - ing an area of 200 hectares (Somay-Altas, 2022).

nodes.question: What has been the primary focus of most studies on bird populations in relation to anthropogenic impacts on oceanic islands?
nodes.answer: Most studies have focused on species richness, abundance, or habitat use, with few addressing physiological changes.

To the best of our knowledge, most studies of bird populations exposed to anthropogenic impacts on oce - anic islands have focused on species richness, abundance, or habitat use, with few addressing questions related to physiological changes [ 41 43]. This study aims to explore the effects of urban and agricultural land use on the morphology and corticosterone levels of two songbird species, the granivorous Small Ground Finch Geospiza fuliginosa and the insectivorous Galapagos Yellow War - bler Setophaga petechia aureola , on San Cristobal Island, Galapagos. We hypothesise that these birds will exhibit differences in hormone concentrations and morphologi - cal traits between natural, agricultural, and urban envi - ronments on San Cristobal Island, given the marked changes in available resources in those environments. Methodology Study area The Galapagos Archipelago comprises 19 main islands (area > 1 km2) and over 100 islets and rocks, with a total area of 7850 km2.
